yes-you-can-replace-your-roof-in-winter-.title: Can You Replace a Roof in the Winter? Yes, But Here’s the Catch
yes-you-can-replace-your-roof-in-winter-.html:
Weather Delays Are More Frequent

Winter brings unpredictable weather, including:

  • Snow and ice accumulation on roofs
  • Freezing rain or sleet
  • Rapid temperature swings

Even light snow or frost can make a roof too slick or dangerous to work on, forcing crews to postpone work until it’s safe again. That means your project could be started, stopped, and restarted multiple times—especially in climates like the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.

At Panda Exteriors, safety comes first, which is why winter work may take longer and require more flexible scheduling to get the job done right.

Fewer Daylight Hours Extend the Timeline

In winter, roofing crews often have 2–3 fewer hours of usable daylight per day compared to spring or fall. That shorter work window can stretch even a simple project into multiple days—especially when paired with cold temps and weather delays.

While our teams work efficiently year-round, winter jobs require extra planning and a little more patience from homeowners.

yes-you-can-replace-your-roof-in-winter-.title: Beat the Next Nor’easter: Why Scheduling Your Roof Replacement Before Deep Winter Saves You Money
yes-you-can-replace-your-roof-in-winter-.html:
The Real Cost of Waiting vs. Proactive Replacement

It’s easy to look at a roof replacement quote and think, “Maybe I can squeeze one more winter out of this roof.” But the real question is:

What could that extra winter cost you?

Here’s how waiting can actually be more expensive long-term:

1. Interior Repairs Add Up Quickly
 One slow, undetected leak can lead to:

  • Ceiling repairs or replacement
  • Repainting rooms
  • Replacing wet or moldy insulation
  • Treating or remediating mold in attics or wall cavities

Suddenly you’re not just paying for a roof—you’re paying for roof + interior work + possible mold treatment.

2. Emergency Repairs Are Always More Expensive
 When a nor’easter tears off shingles and water starts pouring in, you don’t get to choose timing or pricing. Emergency tarping, rush repairs, and last-minute scheduling usually carry premium costs.

3. Energy Loss and Higher Utility Bills
 A worn-out roof system with poor ventilation and compromised insulation can drive your winter heating bills higher. A new, properly installed roofing system can help keep your home more comfortable and efficient.

4. Missed Opportunity to Use Better Weather Windows
 If you delay into the harshest part of winter, you might be stuck waiting for the right conditions—or competing with lots of other homeowners who just discovered leaks. Acting before deep winter gives you:

  • Better schedule options
  • More predictable install days
  • Less stress every time the forecast mentions “nor’easter”

When you stack all of that against the cost of a planned, pre-winter roof replacement, proactive usually wins.

repair-vs-replace-after-a-storm-the-spri.title: Repair or Replace? How to Decide What Your Roof Really Needs
repair-vs-replace-after-a-storm-the-spri.html:
2. Cost Analysis: Repairs vs. Replacement

We know that repairs might seem like the budget-friendly choice, but what about the long-term costs?

Frequent repairs add up. Replacing shingles again and again, dealing with recurring leaks, or patching structural problems can eventually cost more than a full replacement. On the other hand, a one-time investment in a full roof replacement resets the clock and gives you peace of mind for decades.

Full replacement also tends to be more cost-effective per square foot, especially when you factor in newer materials, better warranties, and the opportunity to inspect and fix hidden issues (like rotting decking or compromised underlayment).

If your roof is nearing 15-20 years old, especially with asphalt shingles, it’s often smarter financially to replace rather than repair.

Let’s Break It Down: 8 Factors to Consider

Still unsure? Use this quick guide to help you weigh your options:

  1. Age of the Roof: If it’s over 15–20 years old, replacement is often more cost-effective.
  2. Visual Damage: Curling, cracking, or missing shingles across multiple areas = replacement.
  3. Water Damage: Interior leaks, mold, or sagging ceilings? Replace.
  4. Patchwork History: More than 2–3 repairs in the past few years? Time to stop patching.
  5. Shingle Match: Repaired shingles won’t always blend. If appearance matters, full replacement may be better.
  6. Layer Count: Already have two layers of shingles? You’ll need a tear-off to meet code.
  7. Structural Issues: Rotting decking or sagging? Only a replacement will solve it long-term.
  8. Storm Damage: After major storms, a full inspection is the best next step.

repair-vs-replace-after-a-storm-the-spri.title: Repair or Replace? How to Decide After a Winter Storm Beats Up Your Roof
repair-vs-replace-after-a-storm-the-spri.html:
4. How Insurance and Warranties Play Into the Decision

Winter storm damage is often an insurance issue as much as a roofing issue.

Insurance can help when:

  • The storm caused sudden, accidental damage (wind, hail, fallen limbs, ice dams, etc.).
  • The adjuster agrees the damage is storm-related and not just normal wear and tear.

Depending on your policy, insurance may:

  • Cover repairs to bring the roof back to pre-storm condition, or
  • Help pay for a full replacement if the damage is severe enough or affects a large portion of the roof.

Your deductible and whether you have actual cash value (ACV) or replacement cost coverage will impact how much you pay out of pocket.

Warranties also matter:

  • Manufacturer warranties can be affected if damaged shingles or flashing aren’t repaired properly and quickly.
  • Workmanship warranties from past installations or repairs might help if there were underlying installation issues exposed by the storm.

Panda Exteriors regularly helps homeowners document storm damage, communicate with adjusters, and understand how insurance and warranties apply—so you’re not navigating all of this alone.

repair-vs-replace-after-a-storm-the-spri.title: Should You Repair or Replace Your Roof After a Spring Storm?
repair-vs-replace-after-a-storm-the-spri.html:
Look for hidden damage, not just visible damage

One of the biggest mistakes homeowners make after a spring storm is judging the roof only from the ground. Missing shingles are easy to notice. Hidden storm damage is not.

A roof may have lifted shingles that resealed poorly, hail impact that shortened the life of the material, loosened flashing, or moisture intrusion that has already started affecting the decking and attic. Water does not always drip straight down into the living room right away. It can travel behind walls, across framing, or through insulation before the signs show up indoors.

That is why a professional inspection matters. The real question is not just “Can this be patched?” It is “Will a repair fully restore the integrity of the roof system?” If the answer is no, replacement becomes the smarter option.

15-questions-to-ask-before-you-hire-a-ro.title: How to Choose the Right Roofing Contractor: Questions to Ask Before You Sign
15-questions-to-ask-before-you-hire-a-ro.html:
Also Good to Know

How will you protect my property? Ask how they’ll safeguard landscaping, gutters, siding, and other parts of your home during the job.

What happens if it rains or there’s a delay? Knowing how weather or emergencies are handled helps you plan ahead.

How do you handle clean-up? A quality contractor will leave your property cleaner than they found it—ask if that’s part of the job.

Is a permit required, and do you handle it? Most roof replacements need permits. Make sure the contractor knows the local rules and takes care of this step.

spring-leak-map-how-to-spot-the-failure-.title: Spring Rain = Leak Season: Why Roof Leaks Show Up in March and April
spring-leak-map-how-to-spot-the-failure-.html:
What To Do Immediately If You Notice a Ceiling Stain

A ceiling stain is not just cosmetic. It indicates moisture is reaching insulation, drywall, or framing.

Take these steps:

  • Document the damage with clear photos.
  • Note when the stain grows and what weather conditions were present.
  • Place a container under active drips.
  • If safe, inspect the attic for wet insulation or darkened decking.
  • Run ventilation or fans to reduce interior humidity.

Avoid repainting or patching drywall before identifying the source. Covering the symptom delays the repair and can allow structural damage or mold growth to worsen.

Treat the stain as a diagnostic clue — not the root problem.

The Insurance Factor: Why Spring Matters

Wind-driven rain in spring frequently exposes storm-related damage that occurred during winter.

Lifted shingles, broken seals, and flashing displacement can qualify as storm damage depending on the event and coverage terms. Early documentation improves claim clarity and reduces disputes.

If you suspect storm damage, inspection and documentation should occur before further deterioration changes the damage profile.

spring-roof-inspection-checklist-9-probl.title: The End-of-Winter Roof Survival Checklist
spring-roof-inspection-checklist-9-probl.html:
7 quick checks you can do from the ground

You don’t need to climb to spot meaningful warning signs. Walk the perimeter of your home—ideally on a clear day—and scan the roof from multiple angles.

  1. Missing shingles or bare patches Look for areas that appear darker, uneven, or exposed. Missing shingles can happen from winter wind events, and the underlayment is not meant to stay exposed long-term.
  2. Lifted, curled, or “wavy” shingle edges Shingles should lie flat. If you see rippling lines, corners lifting, or uneven edges, it may indicate wind damage, adhesive failure, or aging shingles.
  3. Damaged or loose flashing Flashing protects the roof at vulnerable transitions—chimneys, skylights, sidewalls, and vent pipes. From the ground, watch for bent metal, separation lines, or sections that look “popped up.”
  4. Staining or discoloration on fascia/soffits Water doesn’t always show up as a roof leak first. Staining under the roof edge may signal gutter overflow, ice-related backing, or water tracking behind trim.
  5. Granules collecting in downspouts or at gutter outlets Asphalt shingles shed granules as they wear. A little is normal, but heavy accumulation (especially after storms) can mean accelerated shingle aging or damage.
  6. Gutters pulling away or sagging Winter ice and snow can stress gutter fasteners. If gutters are separating from the fascia, sagging, or showing overflow marks, water management around the roof edge may be compromised.
  7. Roofline dips or sagging sections Any visible “wave” in the roofline deserves attention. It can indicate moisture damage to decking, structural issues, or long-term wear in a specific area.

Tip: If you have binoculars, use them. You’re not trying to diagnose everything—you’re identifying “something changed” since your last look.

Attic red flags

The attic is often where roof issues show up first, especially after a winter of slow melting and refreezing. Choose a cold morning or a day after recent precipitation if possible, and bring a flashlight.

  • Frost on nails or roof decking Frost can indicate warm, moist air rising into the attic and condensing—often due to ventilation issues, air leaks from the living space, or moisture intrusion. Frost that melts can become “mystery dampness” later.
  • Damp or clumped insulation Insulation should be fluffy and dry. Damp insulation loses performance and can trap moisture against wood surfaces.
  • Musty odors A musty smell is an early warning sign that moisture has been present long enough to create mold-friendly conditions—even if you don’t see visible growth yet.
  • Water stains on rafters or sheathing Dark streaks, rings, or discoloration on wood can point to leaks around flashing, vents, or valleys. Pay special attention to areas under roof penetrations.
  • Light shining through If you can see daylight where you shouldn’t—near chimneys, vent stacks, or roof edges—that’s a strong indicator of a gap that can let water in.

If you find attic moisture, don’t assume it’s “just humidity.” It may be a ventilation imbalance, a bath fan venting into the attic, or a roof penetration that’s starting to fail. Either way, it is worth correcting before spring rains arrive.

ice-dams-101-what-they-are-and-how-to-st.title: Winter-Proof Your Home: Roof, Gutters, and Attic Upgrades That Stop Ice Dams and Heat Loss
ice-dams-101-what-they-are-and-how-to-st.html:
Gutters & Drainage: Keeping Meltwater Moving

Even a great roof can struggle if the gutters can’t do their job. Clogged or undersized gutters contribute directly to ice dams and siding damage.

Key gutter and drainage upgrades that help winter-proof your home:

  • Thorough gutter and downspout cleaning before and during winter so meltwater can drain instead of freezing at the edges of your roof.
  • Gutter guards to keep leaves and debris out, especially in tree-heavy neighborhoods.
  • Properly sized and pitched gutters so water flows smoothly instead of pooling and refreezing.
  • Downspout extensions to carry water away from your foundation and walkways, reducing ice patches and basement moisture.

Panda Exteriors works with roofing and gutters as a system—so when they inspect for winter issues, they’re checking both the top of the roof and where the water is supposed to go when it melts.

Energy Savings & Comfort: The Everyday Payoff

Stopping ice dams and leaks is the obvious benefit—but the everyday comfort gains are just as important:

  • Fewer drafts and cold spots in upstairs rooms
  • More stable indoor temperatures, so your furnace isn’t constantly cycling
  • Lower heating bills because your home holds onto the heat you’re already paying for
  • Less strain on your HVAC system over the long term

Modern roofing and attic systems installed by certified contractors like Panda Exteriors often come with improved ventilation and better energy performance built in—so you’re not just fixing problems, you’re upgrading how your whole home handles winter.

is-your-roof-ready-for-snow-how-to-prepa.title: Winter-Ready Roofs: Why Every Roof Needs a Tune-Up Before First Freeze
is-your-roof-ready-for-snow-how-to-prepa.html:
“It’s New—Do I Really Need a Checkup?”

You might expect years of worry-free performance after a recent replacement, but even younger roofs face real-world stress:

  • Weather wear. High winds, heavy rain, hail, and rapid temperature changes can loosen flashing, lift edges, or weaken sealant lines.
  • Installation settling. As materials expand and contract through their first seasons, small gaps can develop around vents, pipes, nailheads, or skylight perimeters.
  • Debris buildup. Leaves, needles, and branches trap moisture, speed up shingle granule loss, and can clog gutters—inviting overflow at the eaves.
  • Animal activity. Squirrels, birds, and raccoons probe weak points near ridges, eaves, and flashing to create entry paths.

Individually these are minor—but once freeze/thaw cycles begin, moisture expands in tiny openings, turning hairline gaps into real leaks. A short, targeted visit now is often the difference between a simple touch-up and a mid-winter ceiling repair.

is-your-roof-ready-for-snow-how-to-prepa.title: What Cold Weather Does to a Failing Roof (and How to Avoid It)
is-your-roof-ready-for-snow-how-to-prepa.html:
The Freeze-Thaw Cycle: A Silent Roof Killer

One of the most destructive forces your roof faces during winter isn’t visible at first glance—but it’s incredibly damaging over time. It’s called the freeze-thaw cycle.

Here’s how it works:

  1. During the day, snow or ice on your roof begins to melt due to sun exposure or attic heat.
  2. Water seeps into small cracks or worn-out sections of your roof—especially around loose shingles, deteriorated flashing, or nail holes.
  3. At night, temperatures drop, and that water refreezes.
  4. As it freezes, it expands—widening cracks and pushing apart roofing materials.
  5. The cycle repeats daily, slowly prying open the roof layer by layer.

This constant expansion and contraction can severely weaken shingles, dislodge flashing, and open up gaps where moisture and cold air can get in. Over the course of just one winter, the freeze-thaw cycle can do more damage to a failing roof than years of normal wear.

The Hidden Cost of Waiting: Emergency Repairs and Interior Damage

One small leak in fall can turn into a major interior repair by February. Wet ceilings, warped wood, peeling paint, and even structural damage can result when water finds its way inside and freezes repeatedly.

And emergency roofing in winter? That’s often:

  • More expensive due to limited daylight and safety constraints
  • Slower, since icy roofs make working conditions hazardous
  • More disruptive, as you’re dealing with the damage after it’s already inside your home

At Panda Exteriors, we believe in proactive protection. An ounce of prevention in fall is worth a pound of emergency patchwork in January.

best-time-to-go-solar-why-spring-is-a-sm.title: Before School Starts: Why August Is the Perfect Time for Solar Roof Installation
best-time-to-go-solar-why-spring-is-a-sm.html:
Get Ahead of Fall & Winter Energy Bills

While summer electricity bills may spike due to A/C use, fall and winter come with their own set of energy challenges—especially if you rely on electric heat or heat pumps.

Instead of dreading your fall energy statement, imagine watching it drop to just a few dollars—or even seeing a credit—because your home is powered by the sun.

The sooner your system goes live, the sooner your savings begin.

how-to-clean-solar-panels-and-shingles.title: Solar Roof Inspection Checklist: End-of-Summer Maintenance for Maximum Performance
how-to-clean-solar-panels-and-shingles.html:
Electrical System Check: Inverter & Wiring Review

Summer heat can take a toll on electrical components. That’s why it’s crucial to examine your inverter and all visible wiring at the end of the season.

What to check:

  • Inverter display or app for error messages or status changes
  • Breaker panels or disconnects for signs of corrosion or tripped switches
  • Visible conduits and cables for wear, cracking, or sun bleaching

While GAF Solar Shingles are built to endure intense conditions, any issues with your inverter or wiring can significantly reduce system output—or even cause damage to your home’s electrical panel if left unchecked.

Warranty & Documentation Review: Stay Prepared

Now’s a great time to pull out your solar roof documentation and review your warranty terms—especially if your system is still within its first year or two.

Make sure to:

  • Check the GAF warranty coverage for both solar shingles and roof integrity
  • Confirm electrical component warranties (like inverter or panel wiring)
  • Document any issues or irregularities you noticed during your inspection (with photos)
  • Save a copy of your installation paperwork and performance data

If you do discover damage or suspect an issue, having your warranty information and photos ready will make the claim process smoother and faster.

gutters-after-winter-signs-its-time-for-.title: Gutters After Winter: Cleaning, Realignment, and Downspout Flow Tests
gutters-after-winter-signs-its-time-for-.html:
Step-by-step gutter flow test

  • Choose a dry day so you can see exactly where water is going.
  • Clear visible debris first (especially in valleys and near downspouts).
  • Run water from a garden hose into the gutter at the end farthest from the downspout.
  • Watch how quickly it moves toward the downspout and how it exits at the bottom.

What to look for during the test

  • Water pooling or moving slowly: indicates a low spot or poor pitch.
  • Overflow at the front edge: often means a clog downstream or too much roof runoff for that section.
  • Overflow behind the gutter: can indicate improper slope, debris dams, or a gutter pulling away from fascia.
  • Dripping at seams or corners: suggests joint separation or failing sealant.
  • Gurgling or backup at downspouts: signals a blockage—commonly in elbows or underground drain lines.

If the water doesn’t exit cleanly and quickly, the system needs attention—even if it looks fine from the yard.

Gutter guards can make sense when:

  • You have recurring clogs from leaves, pine needles, or roof grit
  • The gutter system is structurally sound (good pitch, secure attachment, minimal seam issues)
  • You want to reduce seasonal cleaning frequency, not eliminate maintenance entirely
  • You’re pairing guards with a tune-up—realignment, resealing, and fastener reinforcement

Guards are most effective when the underlying gutter system is already installed correctly. Adding guards to a sagging or poorly pitched gutter often just hides the problem until overflow returns.

summer-siding-problems-homeowners-ignore.title: Is Your Siding Fading from Sun Exposure? When Summer UV Damage Means It’s Time to Replace
summer-siding-problems-homeowners-ignore.html:
Chalking: A Common Sign of Sun-Damaged Siding

One of the easiest ways to check for siding wear is to look for chalking. Chalking happens when the surface of the siding breaks down and leaves a powdery residue.

You may notice a white, dusty, or powder-like film on your hand after touching the siding. This can be a sign that the outer layer has been damaged by UV rays and weather exposure.

A small amount of chalking can happen with age. But heavy chalking usually means the siding is deteriorating and may be nearing the end of its useful life.

Can You Paint Faded Siding Instead of Replacing It?

In some cases, painting may be an option. However, painting is not always the best solution, especially if the siding is damaged, brittle, warped, or cracked.

Painting can improve appearance, but it will not fix underlying issues like moisture damage, poor installation, loose panels, or failing material.

Before deciding to paint, homeowners should ask:

  • Is the siding still structurally sound?
  • Are there cracks, gaps, or loose panels?
  • Is moisture getting behind the siding?
  • Will paint properly bond to the surface?
  • How long will painting last compared to replacement?
  • Will painting affect the siding warranty?

If the siding is still in good condition and only mildly faded, painting may help refresh the look. But if the siding is failing, replacement is usually the better investment.

Uneven Fading Can Point to Bigger Issues

It is normal for one side of the home to fade faster than another. The side that gets the most direct sun will usually show wear first. But uneven fading can still be a sign that your siding is aging inconsistently.

You may notice:

  • One wall is much lighter than the others
  • Areas under overhangs look darker than exposed areas
  • Replacement panels no longer match the rest of the home
  • The siding looks blotchy or patchy
  • Sun-exposed walls feel more brittle than shaded walls

Uneven fading can make the home look older and may reduce curb appeal. It can also make repairs more difficult because new panels may not blend well with the faded siding.

insurance-paid-roof-replacements-a-simpl.title: Insurance Roofing in Spring: The Homeowner’s Field Guide to Wind and Hail Claims
insurance-paid-roof-replacements-a-simpl.html:
The 10-Photo Documentation Checklist

If you suspect storm damage, your goal is to create a clear, time-stamped record that connects the condition of your home to a specific weather event. Weak documentation is one of the biggest reasons claims get delayed, denied, or scoped too lightly.

A practical homeowner photo checklist should include wide shots of the front, back, and both side elevations of the home so the full roofline and gutter system are visible. It should also include close-up photos of dents on gutters, downspouts, metal fascia, or vents, ideally with a coin or tape measure for scale. If window screens or other soft metals show signs of impact, photograph those as well.

Inside the home, document any ceiling stains, bubbling paint, or signs of active moisture with both wide shots and close-ups. If it is safe to access the attic, take photos of wet decking, damp insulation, or staining near penetrations. It is also helpful to photograph the downspout discharge area if there is visible erosion or overflow evidence, along with any roofing materials that appear displaced from the ground, such as a missing ridge cap, lifted flashing, or shingles that no longer sit in line.

Collateral evidence is especially important. Gutters, vents, downspouts, and screens can help support the presence and severity of hail or wind damage when shingle damage alone is harder to prove. If temporary protection is needed, take photos before installing a tarp or making any quick repairs whenever possible. Homeowners should also avoid prying up tabs, scraping shingles, or trying to test the roof themselves, since that can create new damage and complicate the claim.

Adjuster Terms Every Homeowner Should Understand

Roof claims move quickly, and the language used during an inspection can directly affect the outcome. Understanding a few common terms makes it much easier to follow the conversation.

Collateral damage refers to storm-related impacts on components other than the field shingles, such as gutters, downspouts, vents, and screens. These signs often help confirm the presence and intensity of hail or wind. Test squares are sample areas on a roof slope where an adjuster counts hail hits or functional defects, then uses that information to estimate the rest of the roof. Discontinuity becomes an issue when replacement shingles cannot reasonably match the existing roof because the product is discontinued or heavily weathered. Repairability refers to whether the roof can be repaired without causing additional damage or compromising the system, which is especially important with older or brittle shingles.

It is also important to understand the term accessories, which includes ridge caps, vents, flashing, pipe boots, drip edge, and other non-field components that are often missed in lighter scopes. The scope itself is simply the line-item estimate that shows what the carrier plans to repair or replace. Even small omissions in that document can turn into major out-of-pocket costs later.

Wear and Tear vs. Storm Damage

Many denials and partial approvals come down to one question: does the carrier believe the condition is storm-related, or does it see it as normal aging and deterioration?

In general, insurance is intended to cover sudden, event-driven damage, not gradual wear from time, sunlight, or deferred maintenance. The practical issue is whether the condition is consistent with a specific storm and whether the damage is functional, meaning it affects the roof’s ability to properly shed water.

This is where claims often get complicated. An older roof can absolutely show normal wear and still have legitimate storm damage at the same time. Those two realities are not mutually exclusive. That is why strong documentation and a thorough inspection matter so much. They help establish what changed because of the storm, what can realistically be repaired, and what may require a more complete solution.

when-the-sun-shines-we-shine-together-yo.title: Your Reasons to Go Solar, parts 2 and 3
when-the-sun-shines-we-shine-together-yo.html:
Protection Against Rising Energy Prices

There is an unpredictability of traditional energy costs and also a dependency on local electric companies when your power does go out. Having your own solar energy can offer stability and protection against inflation.

Increased Property Value

The icing on top when installing solar is its ability to increase the resale value of a home. Many families and individuals are all switching to solar because of the great cost benefits and environmental friendly aspects; therefore, when you switch to solar you are not only doing the afore-mentioned but also increasing the value of your home. There’s nothing like tacking on more to your home’s sale price due to solar panels. A study by Zillow reported that homes with solar panels sell for 4.1% more, on average, than those without, and the increase in resale value is higher in certain cities, like New York. A 4.1% increase may not seem like a lot until you consider the size of the numbers involved — if you’re selling a $500,000 home, that’s an extra $20,500!

Savings from Solar Panel Longevity

The expected lifespan of solar panels means less maintenance time and more energy efficiency. Solar panels have a typical life span of 25 to 30 years. The typical U.S. home changes hands every 13.2 years (according to a 2021 Redfin study), which is half the amount of time most Americans live in their homes. Therefore, you can expect many cost savings due to the long-term durability and minimal maintenance of solar panels.

Environmental Benefits

We all want to try and save our environment as much as possible to make this planet livable and enjoyable for future generations… but did you know that going solar can result in environmental cost savings? If you are concerned with your carbon output, rest assured that by solar-powering your home you can reduce your carbon footprint. Residential solar panels emit around 41 grams of CO2 equivalent emissions per kilowatt-hour of electricity generated. Most of these lifecycle emissions are tied to the process of manufacturing panels and are offset by clean energy production within the first three years of operation. The lifetime emissions of rooftop solar are 12 times less than electricity generated by gas plants and 20 times less than electricity generated by coal. Furthermore, by protecting the earth, you are potentially saving in terms of environmental damages and health costs.

Avoiding Peak Rates with Solar Battery Storage

As you become more familiar with solar energy, you will hear a lot about Time-of-Use (TOU) rates. TOU rates are a dynamic electric rate schedule that adjusts prices based on the time of day and season, aiming to align with grid demands. With TOU plans, homeowners can be charged more when electricity demand is higher (since it’s more expensive to produce) and charged less when demand drops. But with solar energy you can have solar battery storage, which can help YOU save by using stored power during peak rate hours.

Financing Options that Lead to Savings

We understand that solar energy can be a larger investment for some families but don’t want you to feel the burden of that cost when considering an option that can ultimately protect your home and family. The most popular options for switching to solar are solar loans, leases, and Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Solar loans provide financing for solar panels and solar installations. Solar leases and power purchase agreements (PPA) are two payment options with minimal upfront costs. The main difference between a solar lease and PPA is that under a solar lease, you pay a fixed monthly rate, no matter how much energy is generated or consumed. A solar lease bypasses the upfront costs of solar panels and makes monthly lease payments instead to power their homes with solar energy. With a solar lease, the solar company owns the panels, but you use the electricity they generate to power your home. Solar leases lead to lower energy costs because you are creating your own electricity, separate from the grid. A solar PPA is another way to invest in solar without purchasing the panels upfront. Solar PPAs are similar to solar leases because the solar panel company retains ownership of the panels, even though they are installed on your property. The solar company is responsible for maintaining and repairing the solar panels. Both solar leases and PPAs have contracts that run between 15 – 20 years.
